items.title: [perthnow.com.au] Hormuz shock drives electrification, threatens gas and coal exporters
items.content_html: The International Energy Agency’s 2026 outlook says disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is pushing governments and consumers toward domestic energy supplies, electrification and more diverse suppliers. In the IEA’s prolonged-disruption case, oil demand in 2035 could be 4.4 million barrels a day below its stated-policy scenario; electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million barrels a day. The IEA models Australian coal exports falling about 11% by 2035, while a potential gas glut could push prices down. The agency also says inadequate electricity grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow electrification, while higher fuel costs risk stalling recent gains in access to electricity and clean cooking in developing economies. The IEA says governments are increasingly making energy security and affordability central to policy, but its modeled pathways are scenarios, not forecasts. If the conflict reaches a clear end, delayed liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies could reach the market and weigh on oil and gas prices even as buyers rebuild inventories.

items.title: [euronews.com] Harvard study links data-center carbon costs to local power grids
items.content_html: The climate impact of U.S. data centers depends strongly on where they draw electricity: generating the same amount of power emitted more than twice as much carbon in coal-heavy Wyoming as in Oregon, where hydropower is significant, researchers found. A Harvard University study estimated that 403 large U.S. data centers emitted 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide between May 2024 and April 2025. Harvard postdoctoral researcher Gianluca Guidi told PBS that Virginia, Iowa, Oregon and Ohio together account for half the facilities’ electricity use, and that communities hosting them may bear pollution and infrastructure costs without receiving the same benefits. The study did not assess health effects, but Guidi said additional electricity demand can mean more power plants and pollution, along with pressure on local infrastructure.

items.title: [independent.co.uk] Fiji declares monthlong disaster emergency as El Niño drought cuts water supplies
items.content_html: Fiji declared a national state of disaster on Nov. 18 as an El Niño-linked drought caused widespread water shortages. Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said the measure lets the government mobilize resources and coordinate aid. Officials allocated 20 million Fijian dollars from existing funds for emergency water supplies for families and farmers. The declaration runs for one month and can be extended or revoked on advice from the National Disaster Risk Management Council. The Fiji Meteorological Service forecast below-normal rainfall from November through April 2027 and above-normal daytime temperatures through January across most of the country. The U.S. Climate Prediction Center put the chance of a strong-to-very-strong El Niño from January through March at more than 79%, while Australian officials said in June the event could become one of the strongest in seven decades.

items.title: [atomic-energy.ru] Russian-built Rooppur reactor sends first 370 MW to Bangladesh grid
items.content_html: Bangladesh’s first nuclear power reactor began supplying electricity to the national grid on Nov. 17, when Unit 1 at the Russian-built Rooppur plant was synchronized with the grid at about 40% of its rated power. Its generator produced 370 megawatts at synchronization, said Alexey Likhachev, director general of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom. The 1,200-MW unit is undergoing a staged startup, with further increases in power and testing required before commercial operation. Rooppur’s two reactors are designed for a combined 2,400 MW; the second unit is expected to follow in 2027.

items.title: [news.un.org] COP31 ministers face deadlock over fossil fuels, finance and science
items.content_html: Ministers at the United Nations COP31 climate summit in Antalya remained deadlocked Wednesday over a final agreement, with 21 issues unresolved and only days left before the conference’s scheduled close Friday, Nov. 20. Disputes include whether to call for a transition away from fossil fuels, how to fund climate adaptation and whether to set a global electrification goal. A draft political deal released Monday included competing proposals on fossil fuels, climate finance, the 1.5°C goal, science and trade. Turkey’s proposal to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use to 35% by 2035 has support from 75 countries, but some governments oppose including it in the final text. Countries also disagree over when the next assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed climate science body, should be ready. Vulnerable countries want them before the 2028 global review, while others favor 2029. Ministers met informally Wednesday to seek compromises; a revised draft was expected Thursday.

items.title: [european-union.europa.eu] EU agrees to streamline permits for renewable projects and power grids
items.content_html: The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on Nov. 18 to speed up permitting for renewable energy projects, electricity grids and storage facilities, aiming to reduce construction delays and strengthen energy security. The changes also cover recharging stations and authorizations for new electricity and gas infrastructure. The agreement streamlines deadlines for approvals and grid connections and provides for digital portals to handle applications. Both institutions must still endorse and formally adopt it after a legal and linguistic review; member states will then have 18 months to incorporate the directive into national law.

items.title: [pv-magazine.com] Moment Energy launches certified second-life battery system for businesses

It has UL safety certifications and independent verification under U.S. foreign-entity sourcing rules, which the company says could qualify it for federal investment tax credits from 2027. Orders opened Nov. 18, 2026, with first deliveries expected in the first quarter of 2027. Nova can discharge at full power for two hours; Moment says its compact design is intended for sites including hospitals, airports and manufacturing facilities.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UK climate advisers warn weaker EV rules could add 8.4m tonnes of CO2 a year
items.content_html: The UK’s Climate Change Committee warned that loosening electric-vehicle sales rules could add 8.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year by the next decade and make the country likely to miss legally binding climate targets. The government is consulting on lowering the zero-emission vehicle requirement, which currently requires zero-emission vehicles to account for 80% of new car sales by 2030 and 100% by 2035. The committee says the rules account for the largest share of planned emissions cuts through 2037; weakening them would require comparable reductions elsewhere to meet the carbon budget for 2033-37. Its chair, Nigel Topping, also warned that reducing the targets would increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets, while the government says the consultation will not change its stated phaseout dates for petrol and diesel vehicles.

items.title: [canarymedia.com] Google backs $500 million Oregon geothermal project for data centers
items.content_html: Google has agreed to buy 50 megawatts of power from Quaise Energy’s proposed Project Obsidian geothermal plant near Oregon’s Newberry Volcano, with deliveries to three Google data centers in The Dalles expected as early as 2030. Quaise and Google did not disclose the sale price, but Quaise valued the agreement at more than $500 million, according to Canary Media and The Wall Street Journal. The deal is the first commercial power purchase announced for a superhot-rock geothermal project. Quaise plans to use conventional drilling in the project’s first phase and introduce its experimental millimeter-wave drilling in a later phase. The technology aims to reach hotter, deeper rock, but the project remains under development, and the experimental method has not been used at commercial scale. The project will also require a new transmission line to connect the site to the grid.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] Earthshot Prize names five climate innovators in Mumbai, awards £1 million each
items.content_html: Prince William, Prince of Wales, announced five winners of the 2026 Earthshot Prize in Mumbai on Nov. 17, awarding each £1 million ($1.3 million) to expand environmental projects. The recipients were Indian electric-vehicle maker Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, campaign group PFAS-Free France, Niue Ocean Wide Trust, offshore wind company Ørsted and Bhutan, which was recognized for forest conservation. They were selected from 15 finalists working on clean transport, pollution, marine protection, renewable energy and conservation. The awards coincided with the United Nations COP31 climate talks, where countries have struggled to agree on fossil fuels and climate finance. A U.N. report released in October said the world was on course to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius warming threshold. William called for urgent action, saying, “They will not judge us by the promises we made, but by the world we leave behind”.

items.content_html: The World Bank Group announced more than $6.9 billion in climate and development investments at the COP31 summit in Antalya on Nov. 17. The package is expected to mobilize $10.7 billion in private capital across agriculture, manufacturing, infrastructure and renewable energy. In Türkiye, an agricultural operation aims to expand farmers’ access to finance and markets, strengthen supply chains and help cut emissions from production. It adds official integration with the Home Assistant smart home platform, as well as a local mode in which the app and battery communicate over the home network without using the EcoFlow cloud. The rollout is expected to take about a week. Older Stream models initially get these features only if users operate them together with a 5000-series device. In local mode, real-time monitoring and basic controls remain available. Home Assistant can also change settings through the connection, provided users grant the relevant permission.

items.title: [rapporteur.com] France's fusion plan backs €22bn ITER, which will not generate electricity
items.content_html: France’s new fusion roadmap centers on the €22 billion International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) in southern France, which is designed to test fusion, not generate electricity. France aims to develop technologies for a European pilot plant by 2035. Its strategy also relies on the WEST tokamak at Cadarache and the Laser Mégajoule facility near Bordeaux. ITER’s current plan calls for deuterium-deuterium fusion operations in 2035, following years of schedule changes. Its experimental target is 500 megawatts of fusion power for at least 400 seconds, using 50 megawatts of plasma-heating power. The revised plan was announced in June 2025.

items.title: [gwec.net] Ember analysis says adding wind cuts reliable power costs 18%
items.content_html: Adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the modeled median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember published with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC). The combination reduces storage needs because wind and solar output vary at different times and across seasons. Ember estimated that three-quarters of global electricity demand could be met at the 90% threshold for under $100/MWh with wind, compared with half using solar and batteries alone. The analysis also examines the economics of planned fossil-fuel capacity: of 845 gigawatts of coal and gas plants in planning, 706 GW are in regions where firm renewable electricity with backup could cost less than $100/MWh. Ember said it modeled hourly weather from 2015 through 2024 against constant demand and described the results as a stress test, not a forecast.

items.title: [france24.com] COP31 draft calls for immediate fossil-fuel shift as nations remain divided
items.content_html: A first draft of the COP31 climate summit’s political agreement in Antalya calls for an immediate shift away from fossil fuels and increased adaptation funding. Reports describe deadly glacier flooding in Nepal and wildfires in Europe. Australia released the text on Nov. 16 for negotiations among nearly 200 countries; it includes competing proposals to “transition away” from fossil fuels or phase them out, but either could be removed before an agreement is reached. The draft also proposes at least $120 billion a year for adaptation in developing countries by 2035. Climate campaigners say it lacks a clear process for advancing fossil-fuel roadmaps and that the proposed funding would cover less than a third of estimated needs. The proposed electricity target has also drawn criticism because the text does not require the added power to come from renewable sources. Negotiators must reach consensus before the summit’s scheduled close on Nov. 20. Australia’s climate change and energy minister and lead negotiator, Chris Bowen, expects further revisions as ministers negotiate the disputed language.

items.title: [utilitydive.com] US orders Michigan coal plant to stay open despite court ruling
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The U.S. Energy Department issued a seventh emergency order requiring the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell coal plant near Grand Rapids, Michigan, to keep operating for another 90 days, through mid-February 2027, despite a federal appeals court ruling in September that an earlier order was unlawful. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the plant is needed to prevent blackouts and maintain reliable electricity supplies; the department cited lessons from Winter Storm Fern and other events during the 2026 Arctic cold period. The plant had been scheduled to retire in May 2025. Michigan and other states, along with environmental groups, challenged the earlier orders, arguing there was no qualifying emergency. The appeals court agreed, and the Energy Department has asked the full court to rehear the case. That request remains pending as the new order takes effect.

items.title: [phys.org] COP31 nations split over 1.5°C goal as threshold nears
items.content_html: Halfway through the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, countries are divided over whether to keep the 1.5°C warming limit as a central goal after the United Nations said in September that crossing it was imminent and unavoidable. Global temperatures have risen about 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. Some countries want the summit’s final decision to reaffirm 1.5°C as the “right goal” and call for temperatures to return below that limit as soon as possible. Other negotiators, including members of the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, are pushing to weaken or remove references to the target. Scientists say reversing an overshoot would require sharp emissions cuts and large-scale carbon removal over decades; University of Exeter climate scientist Pierre Friedlingstein described that prospect as “extremely ambitious”.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Federal memo warns freshwater pressures threaten Canada’s long-term security
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.
